title: Accidental death in police cell prompts policy changes; Intoxicated man fell, hit his head
article: The Blood Tribe Police are changing several policies on how prisoners are supervised in the wake of the accidental death of a man in their custody.
Curtis Justin Mills died June 1, 2011, several hours after falling and hitting his head on the concrete floor of a cell at Blood Tribe police headquarters in Stand Off.

In a fatality inquiry report released Monday, provincial court Judge Paul Pharo recommended that cellblock guards more closely monitor prisoners who have been hurt and provide video recordings of any injuries to help paramedics make a more accurate diagnosis.
Police Chief Lee Boyd said the department has already adopted some of Pharo's seven recommendations and is in the process of trying to implement the others.
Mills, 48, was a registered sex offender who was required to report annually to police for a review.
He was arrested the previous day at noon when he showed up at headquarters intoxicated.
Officers put Mills in a cell, intending to release him the next morning when he would be sober enough for his interview.
Mills' detention was uneventful until about 10: 30 p.m., when a civilian guard and a constable opened his cell to give him a meal.
"At that time, Mr. Mills took a step back and fell straight backwards, without making any attempt to break the fall, and struck the back of his head on the concrete floor," states the judge's report.
The guard immediately called EMS and paramedics arrived within five minutes.
During an examination that lasted nearly 15 minutes, Mills was coherent, able to stand and had acceptable vital signs.
He vomited twice while paramedics were there - which can be a sign of a head injury.
However, vomiting is also a sign of alcohol withdrawal, which paramedics considered to be the more likely possibility given Mills' history of abuse.
Just after 11 p.m., Mills asked to go back to his cell and declined a visit to the hospital.
Shortly after 4: 30 a.m., the guard asked a police officer to enter Mills' cell and check on him because he hadn't moved for some time.
The officer determined Mills wasn't breathing and paramedics declared him dead a few minutes later.
Mills died from an epidural hematoma: Bleeding on his brain that wouldn't have been apparent during the initial exam, but would have rendered him unconscious sometime after.
"After a lucid period, there is usually a gradual deterioration as the blood pressure in the skull increases," the judge wrote.
Pharo recommended closer monitoring of prisoners who have suffered a head injury, to detect symptoms before the injury turns fatal.
The Blood Tribe Police policy is to check a prisoner's condition every 15 minutes and make a notation in a log book.
The guard made regular checks throughout the night - but mainly by viewing Mills on a video monitor at the control station.
An investigator found the guard got up and looked through the window of Mills' cell on only two occasions.

"The BTPS cellblock monitoring policy should be amended and upgraded to make it clear that a 15-minute prisoner 'check' means a visual check for signs of life performed by having a guard or matron look through the cell door window, rather than a check made solely by the video monitor," Pharo wrote.
In cases when police know the prisoner has been injured, guards should check even more frequently, the judge recommended.
"We implemented that recommendation prior to the fatality inquiry to ensure that's happening," Boyd said.
The judge also recommended that Blood Tribe police show paramedics, whenever possible, video footage of the incident that caused the injury.
Video surveillance footage from inside the cellblock is already archived on a server. Boyd said police are working with their supplier to develop a way to quickly retrieve footage when it's needed.
"If that can be done reasonably, we'll implement that," he said.
